name: ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene)
chemical_makeup: Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene — an amorphous terpolymer of acrylonitrile (chemical resistance, rigidity), polybutadiene rubber (impact toughness) and styrene (processability and gloss)
summary: The classic engineering thermoplastic: tough, impact-resistant, usable near 95-100 °C and uniquely acetone-smoothable. In exchange it is the hardest of the commodity three to print — high shrinkage, real warping and delamination without a heated enclosure, poor UV life, and styrene fumes that demand ventilation.

printing.notes: Print with part cooling essentially off (the BCN3D TDS specifies fan off); active cooling causes warping and interlayer cracking, so use light fan only for bridges and steep overhangs. A heated, draft-free enclosure is effectively mandatory for anything beyond small parts — a passive enclosure suffices for most hobby work, which is why heated_chamber_required is false rather than true. Legacy profiles run 20-60 mm/s; enclosed modern machines push 80-150 mm/s, still slower than PLA/PETG to manage shrinkage. Bed temperature scales with part footprint. Hardened nozzle only for filled ABS grades.

methods: print directly from a heated drybox
drying.dryness_validation: No popping/crackling or steam at the nozzle; smooth glossy extrusion free of micro-bubbles; no fine hairs or fuzz on printed walls
drying.notes: Bambu recommends 80 °C for 8 h. Because ABS keeps absorbing moisture on the shelf, desiccant storage is an ongoing practice rather than a pre-print step; wet ABS bubbles and bonds poorly between layers.

storage.recommendations: Airtight box or drybox with desiccant at all times, not just before printing; more sensitive to ambient humidity swings than PLA

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades: budget $18-22, mid $20-24, premium $28-35 per kg. ABS no longer undercuts PETG — budget PETG now often matches or beats it.

recommended: cosmetic parts finished by acetone vapour smoothing
parts needing higher HDT than PLA or PETG
snap-fit and interlocking assemblies (good fatigue resistance)
prototypes intended for sanding and painting
not_recommended: UV-exposed outdoor parts (yellows and embrittles — use ASA instead)
printing in an unventilated occupied room (styrene fumes)
open-frame printers or beginners (warping and delamination)
storage or use in humid conditions without drying

properties.notes: Density 1.04-1.06 g/cm³ — the lightest of the commodity three, so a 1 kg spool yields noticeably more part volume. BCN3D TDS: HDT 99 °C, Vicat softening 105 °C, yield 45 MPa, operating limit 85 °C. Highest shrinkage of the three, and larger/thicker parts trend to the top of the band.

compatibility.notes: Welds permanently to ASA (same styrenic family, near-identical bonding) and bonds moderately to PC — the basis of commercial PC/ABS blends and a common multi-material engineering pairing. HIPS is the classic breakaway/soluble support for ABS: matching print temperatures and dissolvable in D-limonene. Because ABS welds to ASA rather than releasing from it, ASA-supported-by-ABS is a structural pairing, not a clean-release one. ABS pairs badly with PLA and PETG in either direction — its 100 °C bed and 250 °C nozzle deform them, and the chemistries do not fuse.

plate_recommendations.notes: Works at 90-110 °C bed but wants an adhesion aid — Prusa's standard advice is a glue-stick layer on the PEI sheet. Community practice also uses an ABS/acetone slurry as a first-layer promoter (unverified against primary sources). Textured PEI plus a brim and an enclosure is the reliable combination for large flat parts.

emissions.notes: The highest-emitting of the three by a wide margin: Azimi et al. (2016) measured UFP rates roughly 100-1000x those of PLA, with styrene as the named VOC of concern. Print in a well-ventilated space; the ideal setup is an enclosure that contains fumes plus external venting or HEPA+carbon filtration. Ventilate the room without blowing a draft across the print itself.

safety_notes: Styrene is a respiratory irritant and a suspected carcinogen with chronic exposure — do not run ABS in an unventilated occupied room. Acetone vapour smoothing adds its own hazards: acetone is highly flammable and needs ventilation away from ignition sources.
additional_notes: For outdoor work choose ASA instead: near-identical printing and mechanical behaviour with vastly better UV resistance.

provenance.conflicts: Shrinkage: Prusa-cited ABS figures quote 1-2 % for large parts while property tables cite ~0.5 % — recorded as a 0.5-1.5 % consensus band with 0.8 % typical. HDT: BCN3D measures 99 °C, Polymaker's table spans 100-118 °C across grades — 99 °C recorded for plain ABS. Bed temperature: Prusa defaults ~100 °C, the BCN3D TDS says 90 °C. Heated chamber: sources describe an enclosure as 'effectively required' for large parts, but since a passive enclosure is normally sufficient, heated_chamber_required is set false and enclosure_recommended true. ABS/acetone slurry as an adhesion aid is community practice, unverified against the cited sources.
